title: SRAM power-up-state PUF (intrinsic mismatch fingerprint and entropy source)
topology: An array of standard 6T SRAM cells read immediately after power-up, before any value is written. Each cell is a pair of cross-coupled inverters; at power-up the cell resolves to 0 or 1 according to the sign of the manufacturing mismatch between its two halves. The spatial pattern of power-up states is a device-unique, repeatable fingerprint (a Physical Unclonable Function response) usable for identification and — after a fuzzy extractor / error-correction step — for secret-key generation. The same array is a dual-use primitive: cells whose mismatch is small enough that noise, not mismatch, decides the power-up state are unstable and their bits are a source of true randomness, so a power-up SRAM can serve both as a PUF (stable cells) and as a TRNG seed source (noisy cells).
spec_class: hardware security primitive — Physical Unclonable Function for device authentication and key storage (and secondary TRNG seed source), where a device-unique, unclonable identity or key is derived from intrinsic CMOS mismatch rather than stored in nonvolatile memory; the design must supply a stable, reproducible response plus error-correction/entropy handling, not any analog-precision spec

pdk_portability.notes: The primitive is portable to any CMOS PDK that has an SRAM bitcell, including sky130 (which provides an open SRAM bitcell / OpenRAM-generated macros). What is PDK-specific is the mismatch distribution that sets the fraction of strongly-biased (stable, PUF-usable) versus weakly-biased (noisy, TRNG-usable) cells, plus the reliable power-up read behavior; these depend on device threshold mismatch, ramp rate, and retention characteristics and must be characterized on sky130 silicon. Response stability over temperature, voltage, and aging must be measured on the target PDK to size the error-correction budget; do not port a bit-error-rate or entropy figure from another node or from an FPGA-embedded-SRAM measurement.

sizing_approach: The array is built from the PDK's standard 6T bitcell rather than custom-sized transistors — the PUF exploits the cell's intrinsic random mismatch, so it deliberately does not equalize the two halves. The sizing decisions are at the system level: choose the array size (number of cells) large enough that, after discarding unstable cells and applying error correction, enough stable bits remain to meet the required key length with margin against the measured intra-device bit-error-rate (from temperature/voltage/aging drift); and size the fuzzy-extractor / error-correcting-code (e.g. a helper-data scheme with BCH or repetition-plus-BCH coding) to the worst-case measured BER so the reconstructed key is reliable while the helper data leaks acceptably little entropy. For the TRNG use, identify the noisy-cell subset and treat only those bits as an entropy source subject to SP 800-90B validation. Provision extra cells for enrollment/discard and for aging margin.
layout_idioms: use the PDK's characterized standard SRAM bitcell array layout unchanged — the mismatch that gives each cell its identity comes from the normal cell, so PUF cells are deliberately NOT hand-matched or common-centroid-laid-out
controlled, repeatable power-up: a clean supply ramp and a guaranteed no-write read path so the fingerprint is read before any programmed value can overwrite the intrinsic state

keep enrollment/reconstruction and helper-data handling logic physically separate from and access-controlled relative to the raw array, so the unclonable response and derived key are not exposed on scan/debug paths
provide a raw-response read path for characterization and, for the TRNG-seed use, a raw-noisy-cell tap for SP 800-90B validation, while gating field access to the reconstructed key

source.citation: D. E. Holcomb, W. P. Burleson, and K. Fu, "Power-Up SRAM State as an Identifying Fingerprint and Source of True Random Numbers," IEEE Transactions on Computers, vol. 58, no. 9, pp. 1198-1210, Sept. 2009 (author-hosted preprint publicly available). Foundational SRAM-PUF/fuzzy-extractor context: J. Guajardo, S. S. Kumar, G.-J. Schrijen, and P. Tuyls, "FPGA Intrinsic PUFs and Their Use for IP Protection," CHES 2007. Entropy/health-testing guidance for the TRNG-seed use: E. Barker et al., NIST Special Publication 800-90B, January 2018.
source.license_or_openness: Holcomb-Burleson-Fu is cited for its power-up-SRAM PUF/TRNG concept and methodology only (no figures or text reproduced); an author-hosted preprint is publicly available (case 1 open-access), with the IEEE Transactions version behind a subscription (case 2). Guajardo et al. is cited (case 2) for the intrinsic-PUF + fuzzy-extractor methodology. NIST SP 800-90B is a public-domain U.S. government standard. No proprietary or NDA'd data is recorded.

notes: SRAM PUFs are attractive because they reuse an existing, well-characterized memory macro with no custom analog cell, but they REQUIRE a fuzzy extractor / error-correcting code to turn a noisy power-up response into a stable key, and the helper data must be designed to leak little entropy. Response drift over temperature, voltage, and aging sets the error-correction budget and must be measured on silicon. When the same array is used as a TRNG seed source, only the unstable (noise-dominated) cells count as entropy and their output is still subject to conditioning and SP 800-90B health testing. For an oscillator-based unclonable-identity alternative that avoids the power-up-read requirement, see ro-puf; for pure entropy sources see ring-oscillator-jitter-trng and metastability-trng.
